questions.question: What is the primary mechanism used by Bubble Sort to order elements?
options: Selecting the smallest element and moving it to the front
questions.explanation: Bubble sort works by stepping through the list, comparing adjacent elements and swapping them if they are in the wrong order.

questions.question: Bubble Sort has a worst-case time complexity of O(____).
questions.explanation: In the worst case (reverse sorted), Bubble Sort makes n*(n-1)/2 comparisons.

questions.question: Find the bug: for(let i=0; i<n; i++) { for(let j=0; j<n; j++) { if(arr[j] > arr[j+1]) swap(j, j+1); } }
questions.answer: Index out of bounds error at arr[j+1]
questions.explanation: When j equals n-1, j+1 is n, which is out of bounds for an array of size n. The inner loop should go up to n-i-1.

questions.question: Which property makes Bubble Sort suitable for checking if a list is already sorted?
options: It can be optimized to stop early if no swaps occur
questions.answer: It can be optimized to stop early if no swaps occur
questions.explanation: By using a boolean flag to track swaps, Bubble Sort can finish in O(n) time for a sorted list.

questions.question: Bubble sort is a ____ algorithm, meaning it preserves the relative order of equal elements.
questions.explanation: Stable algorithms ensure that items with the same key remain in the same relative order.

questions.question: In a Bubble Sort pass, what is the maximum number of positions a small element (turtle) can move toward the beginning of the list?
questions.explanation: Large elements 'bubble' to the end quickly, but small elements move only one position left per pass.

questions.question: The auxiliary space complexity of Bubble Sort is O(____).
questions.explanation: Bubble Sort is an in-place algorithm and requires only a constant amount of extra memory.

questions.question: Is the following stable? if(arr[j] >= arr[j+1]) swap(j, j+1);
questions.explanation: Swapping equal elements (>=) breaks the relative order, making the algorithm unstable.

questions.question: How many passes are required to sort an array of 5 elements in the worst case?
questions.explanation: Standard Bubble Sort requires n-1 passes to guarantee the list is sorted.

questions.question: A variant of Bubble Sort that sorts in both directions is called ______ Sort.
questions.explanation: Cocktail Shaker sort moves both ways to handle 'turtles' more efficiently.

questions.question: Which of these is the best-case time complexity of Bubble Sort?
questions.explanation: With a swap-tracking optimization, the best case (sorted array) is linear.

questions.question: Bubble Sort is a _____-based sorting algorithm.
questions.explanation: It relies on comparing pairs of elements to determine their order.

questions.question: Identify the logic error: if(arr[j] < arr[j+1]) swap(j, j+1); for an ascending sort.
questions.explanation: To sort ascending, we should swap if the left element is GREATER than the right.

questions.question: What happens to the largest element in the first pass of Bubble Sort?
options: It moves to the first position
It moves to its correct sorted position at the end
questions.answer: It moves to its correct sorted position at the end
questions.explanation: The largest element 'bubbles' to the very last index in the first full iteration.

questions.question: Bubble sort is an __-place sorting algorithm.
questions.explanation: It sorts the original array without requiring a copy.

questions.question: If an array is [1, 2, 3, 5, 4], how many swaps will an optimized Bubble Sort perform?
questions.explanation: Only 5 and 4 need to be swapped to sort the array.

questions.question: In Bubble Sort, elements that are much smaller than their correct position are called ______.
questions.explanation: Small elements move slowly to the left, hence the name turtles.

questions.question: Does Bubble Sort require recursion?
questions.explanation: While it can be implemented recursively, it is naturally an iterative algorithm.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT true about Bubble Sort?
options: It has O(n log n) average complexity
questions.answer: It has O(n log n) average complexity
questions.explanation: Average and Worst case are both O(n^2).

questions.question: The total number of comparisons in Bubble Sort for 'n' elements is always ________.
questions.explanation: The math formula for total comparisons in a full nested loop without early exit is n(n-1)/2.

questions.question: What is the prerequisite for using Binary Search on an array?
options: Array must be of even length
questions.explanation: Binary search relies on the property that elements are ordered to eliminate half the search space.

questions.question: Binary Search has a time complexity of O(____).
questions.explanation: The search space is halved in every step, leading to logarithmic complexity.

questions.question: Identify the overflow risk: int mid = (left + right) / 2;
questions.answer: Integer overflow if left + right exceeds max int
questions.explanation: Adding two large integers can exceed the data type limit. Use left + (right - left) / 2.

questions.question: Binary Search follows which algorithmic paradigm?
questions.explanation: It divides the problem into smaller subproblems (halves) to find the solution.

questions.question: In a sorted array of 1024 elements, the maximum number of comparisons is ____.
Infinite loop check: if(target < arr[mid]) right = mid; else left = mid;
questions.answer: Infinite loop if left and right are adjacent
questions.explanation: If mid doesn't change, the search space never shrinks. Use mid-1 and mid+1.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of iterative Binary Search?
questions.explanation: Iterative binary search uses only a few pointers and no extra memory relative to n.

questions.question: The space complexity of recursive Binary Search is O(____).
questions.explanation: Recursive calls take up space on the call stack.

questions.question: To find the first occurrence of a number in an array with duplicates, what do you do when arr[mid] == target?
options: Search only in the right half
Search only in the left half
Update result to mid and search left
questions.answer: Update result to mid and search left
questions.explanation: To find the earliest occurrence, you record the index and continue searching toward index 0.

questions.question: Binary search is used to implement ______ in databases.
questions.explanation: B-Tree indexes use binary search logic for fast record lookup.

questions.question: If an element is not present, Binary Search usually returns:
questions.explanation: Standard practice is to return -1 to indicate the target is not in the collection.

questions.question: Binary search can be applied to a monotonic ________.
questions.explanation: This is called 'Binary Search on Answer', used in optimization problems.

questions.question: What is wrong: while(left <= right) { mid = ...; if(arr[mid] == target) return mid; if(arr[mid] < target) left = mid; }
questions.answer: Missing right pointer update and potential infinite loop
questions.explanation: If target is not found, the logic provided only handles the 'left' case poorly.

questions.question: Why is Binary Search not suitable for Linked Lists?
options: Random access is O(n) in linked lists
questions.answer: Random access is O(n) in linked lists
questions.explanation: Binary search requires fast random access (O(1)) to calculate mid, but lists require traversal.

questions.question: Lower bound is the first index where arr[i] is ____ than or equal to target.
questions.explanation: Lower bound finds the first possible position for the target.

questions.question: In ternary search, we divide the array into how many parts?
questions.explanation: Ternary search uses two midpoints to divide the space into three segments.

questions.question: The time complexity for one step of Binary Search is O(__).
questions.explanation: Calculating mid and comparing takes constant time.

questions.question: Correction needed: while(left < right) {...} to find target in size 1 array.
questions.explanation: With <, an array with one element might not be checked.

questions.question: Which of the following problems can be solved with binary search?
options: Finding the median of two sorted arrays
questions.answer: Finding the median of two sorted arrays
questions.explanation: Binary search can efficiently partition two arrays to find the median.

questions.question: Exponential search starts by checking index ____.
questions.explanation: It starts with 1 and doubles the range until it finds a boundary.

questions.question: What is the primary operation in each pass of Selection Sort?
options: Finding the minimum element in the unsorted part
Inserting an element into its sorted position
Dividing the array into two halves
questions.answer: Finding the minimum element in the unsorted part
questions.explanation: Selection sort works by scanning the unsorted part to find the minimum and swapping it with the first element of that part.

questions.question: Selection Sort has a best-case time complexity of O(____).
questions.explanation: Unlike Bubble or Insertion sort, Selection Sort always performs n^2 comparisons regardless of whether the array is already sorted.

questions.question: Find the logic error for an ascending sort: for(i=0; i<n; i++) { min=i; for(j=i+1; j<n; j++) { if(arr[j] > arr[min]) min=j; } swap(i, min); }
questions.answer: The comparison if(arr[j] > arr[min]) results in a descending sort.
questions.explanation: To sort in ascending order, the condition should be if(arr[j] < arr[min]) to find the smallest value.

questions.question: Selection Sort is generally considered to be:
questions.explanation: Selection sort can swap non-adjacent equal elements, which may change their original relative order.

questions.question: Selection Sort is an __-place sorting algorithm.
questions.explanation: It requires only O(1) auxiliary space, sorting the array within its own memory bounds.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of swaps performed by Selection Sort for an array of size n?
questions.explanation: In each of the n-1 passes, at most one swap is performed to place the minimum element.

questions.question: Selection sort is preferred over other algorithms when the cost of ______ is very high.
questions.explanation: Since it performs a maximum of n-1 swaps, it minimizes write operations compared to Bubble Sort.

questions.question: Identify the performance bug: if(min != i) swap(arr[i], arr[min]); inside the loop. Is it a bug if we remove the 'if'?
questions.answer: No, it's not a logic bug, but it causes unnecessary self-swaps.
questions.explanation: Checking if(min != i) prevents swapping an element with itself, saving execution time.

questions.question: How many comparisons are made in the first pass of Selection Sort for 10 elements?
questions.explanation: The first element is compared with the remaining n-1 (9) elements.

questions.question: Selection sort belongs to the ______ class of sorting algorithms.
questions.explanation: It uses comparisons between elements to decide their order.

questions.question: Which sort is Selection Sort most similar to in terms of complexity?
questions.explanation: Both have O(n^2) worst-case time complexities.

questions.question: In selection sort, after 'k' passes, the first 'k' elements are in their ______ positions.
questions.explanation: Selection sort guarantees that each pass places one element in its absolute correct position.

questions.question: Is selection sort recursive? void sort(int a[], int i, int n) { if(i==n) return; int m=findMin(a,i,n); swap(a[i], a[m]); sort(a, i+1, n); }
questions.answer: No error, this is a correct recursive implementation of selection sort.
questions.explanation: Selection sort can be implemented recursively by passing the index of the unsorted start.

questions.question: What is the memory complexity of Selection Sort?
questions.explanation: It is an in-place algorithm using constant auxiliary space.

questions.question: Selection sort scans the ______ part of the array to find the minimum.
questions.explanation: The array is logically divided into a sorted prefix and an unsorted suffix.

questions.question: In what scenario does Selection Sort perform fewer comparisons than Insertion Sort?
options: When the array is reverse sorted
When the array is already sorted
questions.explanation: Selection sort always performs n(n-1)/2 comparisons, while Insertion sort varies based on data.

questions.question: The time complexity of Selection Sort on a linked list is O(____).
questions.explanation: Even on a linked list, we must traverse the unsorted part for each element.

questions.question: Logic Check: Can we find the maximum instead of the minimum?
questions.answer: Yes, finding the maximum and swapping with the end is also selection sort.
questions.explanation: The logic remains the same, just the direction of sorting placement changes.

questions.question: Which algorithm is NOT stable?
questions.explanation: Out of the basic sorts, Selection Sort is the one that is non-stable.

questions.question: Selection sort performs ______ comparisons for an array of size n.
questions.explanation: The arithmetic progression 1+2+...+(n-1) equals n(n-1)/2.

questions.question: How does Insertion Sort build the sorted array?
options: One element at a time by comparisons
By dividing the array in half
questions.answer: One element at a time by comparisons
questions.explanation: Insertion sort takes an element and inserts it into its correct position in the sorted part.

questions.question: Insertion Sort has a best-case time complexity of O(____).
questions.explanation: When the array is already sorted, only one comparison is made per element.

questions.question: Fix the loop: for(i=1; i<n; i++) { key=arr[i]; j=i-1; while(j>=0 && arr[j] < key) { arr[j+1]=arr[j]; j--; } arr[j+1]=key; }
questions.answer: The condition arr[j] < key sorts in descending order.
questions.explanation: For ascending order, use arr[j] > key.

questions.question: Is Insertion Sort stable?
questions.explanation: It does not swap equal elements, preserving their relative order.

questions.question: Insertion Sort is highly efficient for ______ datasets.
questions.explanation: For small N, its low overhead makes it faster than O(n log n) algorithms.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm is used by Shell Sort as a sub-step?
questions.explanation: Shell sort is an optimization of insertion sort using gaps.

questions.question: An algorithm that processes its input element by element is called an ______ algorithm.
questions.explanation: Insertion sort can sort a list as it receives it.

questions.question: Why is j=i-1; while(j>0) { ... } a bug?
questions.answer: It misses the element at index 0.
questions.explanation: The loop should be while(j >= 0) to check all elements in the sorted part.

questions.question: Worst-case complexity of Insertion Sort occurs when:
questions.explanation: Every element must be compared and shifted across the entire sorted part.

questions.question: Binary Insertion Sort uses ______ to find the insertion point.
questions.explanation: This reduces comparisons to O(n log n), though shifts remain O(n^2).

questions.question: Average case complexity of Insertion Sort?
questions.explanation: On average, each element is shifted halfway, resulting in quadratic time.

questions.question: Insertion Sort is an ______ algorithm, meaning it takes no extra memory.
questions.explanation: It rearranges elements within the original array.

questions.question: Logic Check: Is key=arr[i] necessary? Can we just swap?
questions.answer: Yes, but using 'key' and shifting is more efficient than repeated swapping.
questions.explanation: Shifting reduces the number of assignment operations from 3 (swap) to 1.

questions.question: Which sort does Python's Timsort use for small runs?
questions.explanation: Timsort is a hybrid of Merge and Insertion sort.

questions.question: Insertion sort is similar to sorting a deck of ______.
questions.explanation: Taking a card and placing it in order among cards already in hand is the classic analogy.

questions.question: Number of inversions in a reverse sorted array of size n?
questions.explanation: Each pair is an inversion, leading to the same count as selection sort comparisons.

questions.question: Complexity when array is almost sorted?
questions.explanation: Minimal shifts are required, resulting in nearly linear time.

questions.question: Can Insertion Sort be used with Linked Lists?
questions.answer: Yes, and it is very efficient as it doesn't require shifting elements.
questions.explanation: It only requires pointer updates, though finding the position is still O(n).

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an in-place sort?
questions.explanation: Standard merge sort requires O(n) auxiliary space.

questions.question: Number of comparisons in best case?
questions.explanation: For a sorted array, i goes from 1 to n-1, performing 1 comparison each.

questions.question: Merge Sort follows which paradigm?
questions.explanation: It recursively splits the array and merges sorted results.

questions.question: Merge Sort has a worst-case complexity of O(____).
questions.explanation: The recurrence relation T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n solves to O(n log n).

questions.question: Base case check: if(low < high) { mid = (low+high)/2; mergeSort(low, mid); mergeSort(mid, high); merge(low, mid, high); }
questions.explanation: The second call should be mergeSort(mid+1, high) to ensure sub-problems shrink.

questions.question: Is standard Merge Sort stable?
questions.explanation: By checking left[i] <= right[j] during merge, equal elements maintain order.

questions.question: Auxiliary space complexity is O(____).
questions.explanation: Merge sort requires a temporary array of the same size as input for merging.

questions.question: Which of the following is an internal sort?
questions.explanation: Wait, Merge Sort is actually the most common choice for External Sorting.

questions.question: Merge sort is preferred for ______ Lists.
questions.explanation: It doesn't require random access and can be implemented in O(1) space for lists.

questions.question: If mid = (low + high) / 2 is used, what is the risk?
questions.explanation: Use low + (high - low) / 2 for safety.

questions.question: Best case complexity?
questions.explanation: Merge sort always performs the same amount of work regardless of order.

questions.question: In the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, 'n' represents the complexity of ______.
questions.explanation: Merging two sorted halves of total size n takes linear time.

questions.question: Depth of the recursion tree?
questions.explanation: Array size is halved at each level, leading to logarithmic depth.

questions.question: Merge sort is NOT an ______ sort in its standard array form.
questions.explanation: It requires O(n) additional space.

questions.question: Logic Check: What happens if low == high in the base case?
questions.answer: Infinite loop or error if recursive call logic is wrong.
questions.explanation: Base case must handle low >= high to stop recursion at single-element arrays.

questions.question: Which algorithm is highly parallelizable?
questions.explanation: The two halves can be sorted independently on different processors.

questions.question: Mergesort is a ______ algorithm.
questions.explanation: It calls itself to sort the halves.

questions.question: Minimum number of comparisons to merge two sorted arrays of size 5?
questions.explanation: When all elements of one array are smaller than all elements of the other.

questions.question: Stability of Merge Sort depends on the ______ step.
questions.explanation: Correct comparison logic in the merge function ensures stability.

questions.question: What if mid = low + (high - low) / 3?
questions.explanation: The logic works, but complexity becomes T(n) = 3T(n/3) + n.

questions.question: Standard Merge Sort uses how much space?
questions.explanation: Calculated based on the temporary array used in the merge function.

questions.question: In-place Merge Sort exists but has ______ overhead.
questions.explanation: It is complex and usually slower in practice despite saving space.

questions.question: What is the heart of the Quick Sort algorithm?
questions.explanation: Partitioning places a pivot in its correct spot and moves smaller elements to the left.

questions.question: Quick Sort average case time complexity is O(____).
questions.explanation: When the pivot splits the array into reasonably equal parts.

questions.question: Worst Case Fix: Pick arr[0] as pivot. How to fix for sorted arrays?
questions.explanation: Always picking the first element leads to O(n^2) for already sorted arrays.

questions.question: Is Quick Sort stable?
questions.explanation: Swaps during partitioning can reorder equal elements.

questions.question: Quick Sort space complexity for the recursion stack is O(____).
questions.explanation: Average stack depth is logarithmic, though worst case is O(n).

questions.question: Which partitioning scheme is typically more efficient?
questions.explanation: Hoare's scheme performs fewer swaps on average.

questions.question: The element used to divide the array is called the ______.
questions.explanation: The entire logic depends on this chosen value.

questions.question: Partitioning logic: if(arr[j] <= pivot) { i++; swap(arr[i], arr[j]); } what if we use < ?
questions.answer: Stability issue or handling equal elements incorrectly.
questions.explanation: Using <= ensures elements equal to the pivot are handled properly.

questions.question: Worst-case complexity of Quick Sort?
questions.explanation: Occurs when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element.

questions.question: Quick sort is an ______ sorting algorithm.
questions.explanation: It performs best when data is in main memory.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT true about Quick Sort?
questions.explanation: Quick Sort is inherently unstable.

questions.question: Hoare partition uses two ______ moving towards each other.
questions.explanation: Pointers 'i' and 'j' start at ends and move inward.

questions.question: Why is tail recursion optimization useful in Quick Sort?
questions.answer: It reduces stack space to O(log n) in the worst case.
questions.explanation: By always recursing into the smaller partition first.

questions.question: Best case happens when pivot is always:
questions.explanation: This ensures the array is split into two equal halves.

questions.question: Quick Sort is a ______ and Conquer algorithm.
questions.explanation: Part of the standard algorithmic trinity: Divide, Conquer, Combine.

questions.question: Complexity when all elements are equal?
questions.explanation: Lomuto partition results in O(n^2) for equal elements, whereas Hoare results in O(n log n).

questions.question: The C++ standard library sort usually uses ______.
questions.explanation: IntroSort starts with QuickSort and switches to HeapSort if recursion depth is too high.

questions.question: What if pivot is picked from mid of array?
questions.answer: Good heuristic, but doesn't guarantee avoiding O(n^2).
questions.explanation: Median-of-three is safer.

questions.question: Space complexity of in-place Quick Sort?
questions.explanation: Technically logarithmic due to the recursive call stack.

questions.question: Randomized Quick Sort has an expected time complexity of O(____).
questions.explanation: Randomization prevents an attacker from providing a worst-case input.

questions.question: What data structure is fundamentally used to implement Heap Sort?
questions.explanation: A heap is a specialized complete binary tree based on the heap property.

questions.question: Heap sort is a _____-based sorting algorithm.
questions.explanation: It compares elements to build the heap and extract the maximum/minimum.

questions.question: Find the error in calculating child index for a 0-indexed array: left = 2*i; right = 2*i + 1;
questions.explanation: In 0-indexed arrays, the left child of node i is at 2i + 1 and the right is at 2i + 2.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Heap Sort?
questions.explanation: Building the heap takes O(n) and extracting n elements takes O(n log n).

questions.question: To sort an array in ascending order, we must build a ____-heap.
questions.explanation: Extracting the maximum element from a max-heap and moving it to the end results in ascending order.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about Heap Sort stability?
questions.explanation: Heap operations can move equal elements across large distances in the array, breaking their relative order.

questions.question: The auxiliary space complexity of Heap Sort is O(____).
questions.explanation: Heap sort is an in-place algorithm using constant additional memory.

questions.question: Does Heapify require recursion to be O(log n)?
questions.explanation: Iterative heapify is more space-efficient by avoiding call stack overhead.

questions.question: Building a heap from an array of size n takes:
questions.explanation: The sum of the heights of nodes in a complete binary tree is O(n).

questions.question: The time complexity of the extraction phase in Heap Sort is O(____).
questions.explanation: Each of the n extractions involves a log n heapify step.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm is guaranteed to be O(n log n) and in-place?
questions.explanation: Merge sort is not in-place, and Quick sort is O(n^2) in worst case.

questions.question: In a max-heap, the root node contains the ______ value.
questions.explanation: The heap property ensures parents are always greater than or equal to children.

questions.question: Bug check: Is parent of index i at floor(i/2)?
questions.answer: Only for 1-based indexing; for 0-indexed, it is floor((i-1)/2).
questions.explanation: Array indexing differences change the parent calculation formula.

questions.question: Which of these is better than Heap Sort on almost sorted data?
questions.explanation: Insertion sort is O(n) for almost sorted data; heap sort remains O(n log n).

questions.question: The maximum height of a heap with n nodes is ____.
questions.explanation: A complete binary tree has logarithmic height.

questions.question: How many leaf nodes are in a heap of n nodes?
questions.explanation: Leaf nodes reside from index n/2 to n-1 in a 0-indexed array representation.

questions.question: Heap sort is primarily an ______ sorting algorithm.
questions.explanation: It requires random access to indices, making it unsuitable for external tape sorting.

questions.question: Can we sort a descending array faster with Heap Sort?
questions.answer: No, it still takes O(n log n).
questions.explanation: Heap building takes O(n), but sorting phase always extracts n elements.

questions.question: In which case is Heap Sort least preferred?
questions.explanation: Heap sort is fundamentally unstable.

questions.question: The time complexity of inserting an element into a heap is O(____).
questions.explanation: Insertion involves placing at the end and 'bubbling up' to the root height.

questions.question: What is the primary objective of Kadane's Algorithm?
questions.explanation: Kadane's algorithm efficiently finds the contiguous subarray with the largest sum.

questions.question: Kadane's Algorithm has a time complexity of O(____).
questions.explanation: It iterates through the array exactly once.

questions.question: Find the error: if(curr_sum < 0) curr_sum = arr[i];
questions.answer: Missing logic: max_sum should be updated before reset.
questions.explanation: If all elements are negative, the algorithm needs careful initialization to max negative value.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of Kadane's Algorithm?
questions.explanation: It only uses two variables to keep track of sums.

questions.question: Kadane's algorithm is an application of ______ programming.
questions.explanation: It solves subproblems (max sum ending at i) to solve the global problem.

questions.question: How does Kadane's handle an array of only negative numbers?
questions.explanation: If properly implemented, it should return the least negative value in a totally negative array.

questions.question: Kadane's is preferred over the brute force O(____) approach.
questions.explanation: Brute force checks every possible starting and ending index.

questions.question: Logic Bug: max_so_far = 0; for(val of arr) { curr += val; if(curr > max_so_far) max_so_far = curr; if(curr < 0) curr = 0; }
questions.answer: Fails if all numbers are negative.
questions.explanation: max_so_far should be initialized to -Infinity or arr[0] to handle negative inputs.

questions.question: If we want to find the actual subarray (indices), what extra variables are needed?
questions.explanation: We need to track where the current sum started to update the global start/end.

questions.question: Kadane's can be modified to find the maximum ______ subarray sum.
questions.explanation: The maximum sum is either Kadane's normal sum or TotalSum - MinKadaneSum.

questions.question: Which problem is Kadane's NOT useful for?
questions.explanation: Dijkstra or Bellman-Ford are used for graph shortest paths.

questions.question: The recursive relation for Kadane's is f(i) = max(arr[i], arr[i] + ____).
questions.explanation: The max sum ending at i is either the element itself or the element plus previous max.

questions.question: What if array is [1, 2, 3]? max_sum should be?
questions.explanation: The whole array is the max sum subarray.

questions.question: Kadane's algorithm is named after Jay Kadane, who was from:
questions.explanation: He invented it during an exploration of a problem posed by Ulf Grenander.

questions.question: Contiguous means that elements must be ______ in the array.
questions.explanation: Non-contiguous subsets would be a different problem (Max Subsequence Sum).

questions.question: Time complexity to find max subarray product?
questions.explanation: A modified Kadane's tracking min and max product handles negative numbers in linear time.

questions.question: Kadane's solves the problem in a single ____.
questions.explanation: Linear time means scanning the array from start to end once.

questions.question: Is Kadane's greedy?
questions.explanation: It makes a greedy choice at each step to either include the element or start fresh.

questions.question: Space complexity of Kadane's?
questions.explanation: Only constant space variables are used.

questions.question: The divide and conquer approach to this problem takes O(____).
questions.explanation: Standard divide and conquer for max subarray sum is less efficient than Kadane's.

questions.question: Dijkstra's algorithm is used to find:
questions.explanation: It calculates the shortest path from one source vertex to all other vertices in a weighted graph.

questions.question: Dijkstra's algorithm cannot handle edges with ______ weights.
questions.explanation: Negative weights can lead to incorrect shortest path calculations because it is a greedy algorithm.

questions.question: Identify the performance bottleneck: Using an array to find the minimum distance node in every step.
questions.answer: O(V^2) complexity; use a Priority Queue instead.
questions.explanation: A Min-Heap/Priority Queue reduces selection time to log V.

questions.question: What is the time complexity with a Binary Heap and Adjacency List?
questions.explanation: Each edge relaxation takes log V time in the priority queue.

questions.question: Dijkstra's algorithm is based on the ______ paradigm.
questions.explanation: It always selects the vertex with the smallest distance value from the set of unvisited vertices.

questions.question: Which algorithm is better than Dijkstra for graphs with negative weights?
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford can handle negative weights and detect negative cycles.

questions.question: In Dijkstra, the distance to the source node is initialized to ____.
questions.explanation: The distance from a node to itself is zero.

questions.question: Bug check: Initializing all node distances to 0.
questions.explanation: Except for the source, all other distances must start as infinite.

questions.question: The process of updating a neighbor's distance is called:
questions.explanation: Relaxation checks if a shorter path to a node exists through the current vertex.

questions.question: Using a Fibonacci Heap, Dijkstra's complexity is O(____).
questions.explanation: Fibonacci heaps offer O(1) amortized decrease-key operations.

questions.question: If all weights are 1, Dijkstra is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: BFS naturally finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

questions.question: Shortest path between nodes in a map application is a classic use of ______.
questions.explanation: Navigation systems use variations of Dijkstra/A* for routing.

questions.question: What if weight(u,v) + dist(u) < dist(v) is missing?
questions.answer: Relaxation won't happen; shortest path won't be found.
questions.explanation: This condition is the core logic of the update step.

questions.question: Which data structure represents the path itself?
questions.explanation: Storing the previous node for each vertex allows path reconstruction.

questions.question: A graph must be ______ (non-cyclic or weighted) for Dijkstra to work properly.
questions.explanation: Dijkstra is specifically for weighted graphs (non-negative).

questions.question: Space complexity of Dijkstra's algorithm?
questions.explanation: We store distances, predecessors, and the visited set for all vertices.

questions.question: Once a vertex is added to the 'visited' set, its shortest distance is ______.
questions.explanation: Greedy choice ensures we never re-evaluate a visited node's distance.

questions.question: Can Dijkstra find the longest path?
questions.explanation: Longest path is NP-Hard for general graphs; greedy approach fails.

questions.question: Dijkstra was a computer scientist from:
questions.explanation: Edsger W. Dijkstra was a Dutch computer scientist.

questions.question: A* algorithm is an extension of Dijkstra that uses a ______.
questions.explanation: Heuristics allow A* to search toward the goal faster than Dijkstra.

questions.question: Counting Sort is an example of which type of sorting algorithm?
questions.explanation: Counting sort does not compare elements against each other; it uses the frequency of values to determine positions.

questions.question: The time complexity of Counting Sort is O(n + k), where k is the ______ of the input data.
questions.explanation: Counting sort's efficiency depends on the difference between the maximum and minimum values in the input.

questions.question: Why would counting sort fail for an array like [1, 2, 10^9]?
questions.answer: Memory limit exceeded for the count array
questions.explanation: Counting sort creates an auxiliary array of size 'k'. If k is very large, it consumes excessive memory.

questions.question: To make Counting Sort stable, which direction should the input array be traversed when placing elements into the output array?
questions.explanation: Traversing backwards ensures that the last occurrence of a value in the original array is placed at the highest available position for that value.

questions.question: The auxiliary space complexity of Counting Sort is O(____).
questions.explanation: It requires an array of size k to store the frequencies (counts) of each distinct element.

questions.question: Logic check: Can Counting Sort handle negative numbers out of the box?
questions.answer: No, because indices cannot be negative.
questions.explanation: To handle negatives, you must shift values by adding the absolute value of the minimum element to all elements.

questions.question: Which of these is a requirement for standard Counting Sort?
options: Inputs must be integers within a known range
questions.answer: Inputs must be integers within a known range
questions.explanation: Since values are used as array indices, they must be discrete integers.

questions.question: After storing counts, we modify the count array such that count[i] contains the ______ count.
questions.explanation: The cumulative count indicates the actual position of the element in the sorted output.

questions.question: If n=100 and k=10000, which algorithm is faster?
questions.explanation: If k is significantly larger than n log n, standard comparison sorts outperform counting sort.

questions.question: Counting sort is used as a subroutine in ______ Sort.
questions.explanation: Radix sort uses counting sort to sort digit by digit.

questions.question: In the stable implementation, output[count[arr[i]] - 1] = arr[i]. Why the '-1'?
questions.explanation: The count represents the 1-based position, so index is count - 1.

questions.question: Is Counting Sort in-place? (Yes/No)
questions.explanation: It requires an auxiliary count array and an output array.

questions.question: Bug hunt: output[count[arr[i]]] = arr[i]; count[arr[i]]++; What is wrong for stability?
questions.answer: It should be count[arr[i]]-- to process duplicates correctly from the back.
questions.explanation: Incrementing would place the first element at the start but wouldn't correctly manage positions for following duplicates without a cumulative sum.

questions.question: Which of the following is true for Counting Sort?
options: It is useful for large strings
questions.explanation: The standard algorithm preserves the order of duplicate keys.

questions.question: For n elements and range k, counting sort is efficient only if k is O(__).
questions.explanation: If k > n, the linear advantage is lost.

questions.question: What is the best case time complexity for Counting Sort?
questions.explanation: Counting sort does not depend on the order of elements, only their values and range.

questions.question: Counting sort is not a comparison sort because it never performs ______ operations between keys.
questions.explanation: It never asks 'Is A < B?'

questions.question: If the count array is [0, 2, 3, 5], what is the cumulative count array?
questions.explanation: Each element is the sum of itself and all previous elements (0, 0+2, 2+3, 5+5).

questions.question: Can counting sort be used to sort objects?
options: Yes, if we use a specific field as the key
questions.answer: Yes, if we use a specific field as the key
questions.explanation: As long as the key is an integer in a range, Counting Sort can reorder the objects.

questions.question: Standard Counting Sort uses ____ total arrays.
questions.explanation: Input array, Count array, and Output array.

questions.question: Linear Search starts searching from which index?
questions.explanation: Linear search scans elements sequentially from the start.

questions.question: The average time complexity of Linear Search is O(__).
questions.explanation: On average, you search through half the array (n/2), which is O(n).

questions.question: Find the bug: for(i=0; i<=arr.length; i++) { if(arr[i] == target) return i; }
questions.answer: Array index out of bounds error
questions.explanation: Loop should be i < arr.length. Using <= tries to access arr[length], which doesn't exist.

questions.question: What is the best-case time complexity of Linear Search?
questions.explanation: The best case is finding the target at the very first index.

questions.question: Linear Search is also known as ______ search.
questions.explanation: Elements are checked one after another in a sequence.

questions.question: Why is Linear Search preferred for small unsorted arrays?
options: It is faster than binary search on small N
It doesn't require the data to be sorted
questions.answer: It doesn't require the data to be sorted
questions.explanation: Binary search requires sorting, which takes O(n log n). For small unsorted data, linear search is simpler and sufficient.

questions.question: The space complexity of Linear Search is O(__).
questions.explanation: It only requires a single loop variable.

questions.question: Does linear search require a break statement inside the if condition?
questions.answer: No, if you return the index immediately.
questions.explanation: Returning from the function automatically stops the search.

questions.question: What happens if there are duplicate targets in the array?
options: It returns the first one found
It returns the last one found
questions.answer: It returns the first one found
questions.explanation: Once it finds a match, it usually returns and exits.

questions.question: A Linear Search can be improved on linked lists by using the ______-to-front heuristic.
questions.explanation: Moving the most recently found element to the front speeds up future searches for the same item.

questions.question: How many comparisons does Linear Search make if the target is NOT in the array?
questions.explanation: It must check every single element before concluding the target is missing.

questions.question: The time complexity of Linear Search on a linked list is O(__).
questions.explanation: One must traverse the list node by node.

questions.question: Is it possible to implement Linear Search recursively?
questions.explanation: Check current, then call function on the remaining array tail.

questions.question: Which of these data structures supports Linear Search?
questions.explanation: Any collection that allows sequential access can be searched linearly.

questions.question: If target is not found, Linear Search typically returns ____.
questions.explanation: Common convention to indicate failure in search functions.

questions.question: Sentinel linear search reduces the number of ______ per iteration.
questions.explanation: By putting the target at the end, you don't need to check if the index is within bounds inside the loop.

questions.question: Linear search is the only option when searching in an ______ collection.
questions.explanation: Without order, more advanced algorithms like Binary Search cannot be used.

questions.question: If you use a while loop for linear search, when should you increment the counter?
questions.answer: At the end of the loop body
questions.explanation: Incrementing too early skips the first element.

questions.question: What is the probability of finding an element in the middle (n/2) index?
questions.explanation: Assuming target is in the array and uniform distribution, any index has 1/n chance.

questions.question: Linear search is O(1) in the ______ case.
questions.explanation: Finding it at the first check is constant time.

questions.question: What problem does Moore's Voting Algorithm solve?
questions.explanation: It identifies an element that appears more than floor(n/2) times in an array.

questions.question: The time complexity of Moore's Voting Algorithm is O(__).
questions.explanation: It requires one pass to find a candidate and another pass to verify it.

questions.question: Does finding a candidate guarantee that it is the majority element?
questions.explanation: The algorithm only finds a candidate. If no majority element exists, the candidate might be wrong. A second verification pass is mandatory.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of Moore's Voting Algorithm?
questions.explanation: It only uses two variables: a candidate and a counter.

questions.question: The counter in Moore's algorithm ______ when the current element is different from the candidate.
questions.explanation: Equal elements 'vote' for the candidate, different ones 'vote' against.

questions.question: Why initialize count to 0 and candidate to null?
questions.answer: To correctly process the first element.
questions.explanation: When count is 0, the next element becomes the candidate.

questions.question: If an array is [3, 3, 4, 2, 3], what is the candidate found after the first pass?
questions.explanation: 3 has 3 votes, canceling out 4 and 2. Result is 1 vote for 3.

questions.question: The Boyer-Moore voting algorithm is ______ because it only tracks one element at a time.
questions.explanation: It assumes the current leader is the global leader until proven otherwise by cancellation.

questions.question: If you need to find an element that appears > n/k times, how many candidates do you need to track?
questions.explanation: Generalization of the algorithm (Misra-Gries) tracks k-1 candidates.

questions.question: The second pass in Moore's Voting Algorithm involves ______ elements.
questions.explanation: Verifying if the candidate actually appears more than n/2 times.

questions.question: In which case does Moore's algorithm fail to return the majority element correctly without a second pass?
options: When no element occurs > n/2 times
When all elements are the same
questions.answer: When no element occurs > n/2 times
questions.explanation: If no majority exists, it will still output a candidate, which is misleading.

questions.question: Moore's algorithm is much faster than the O(____) sorting-based solution.
questions.explanation: Sorting and picking mid is n log n, Moore's is linear.

questions.question: Bug hunt: if(arr[i] == candidate) count++; else count--; What is missing?
questions.answer: The check if(count == 0) to reassign the candidate.
questions.explanation: Without reassignment, the first candidate is tracked for the whole array.

questions.question: Array size is 10. How many times must the majority element appear?
questions.explanation: Strictly greater than n/2. 10/2 = 5, so 6 is the minimum.

questions.question: Moore's algorithm processes elements in a ______ pass.
questions.explanation: The candidate search is one pass.

questions.question: Space complexity if we use a Hash Map to solve majority element?
questions.explanation: Hash map stores counts for all distinct elements, which can be up to n.

questions.question: Majority means appearing more than ______ percent of the time.
questions.explanation: Majority is strictly more than half.

questions.question: Can Moore's algorithm find the mode of any array?
questions.explanation: It only works if the mode is a majority (>50%).

questions.question: Who invented this algorithm?
options: Robert S. Boyer and J Strother Moore
questions.answer: Robert S. Boyer and J Strother Moore
questions.explanation: It was published in 1981.

questions.question: If we find two candidates for > n/3 case, the algorithm is known as the ______-Moore generalization.
questions.explanation: Refers to the pair who published it.

questions.question: How many pointers are typically required to reverse a singly linked list iteratively?
questions.explanation: You need 'prev', 'current', and 'next' pointers to reverse connections without losing the rest of the list.

questions.question: The time complexity to reverse a linked list of size n is O(__).
questions.explanation: Every node must be visited and updated once.

questions.question: Identify the bug: curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = curr.next;
questions.answer: Lost reference to the original next node
questions.explanation: Once you set curr.next to prev, the link to the next node is broken. You must store next = curr.next first.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of reversing a linked list iteratively?
questions.explanation: It only uses a few temporary pointer variables.

questions.question: In the recursive approach, the space complexity is O(__) due to the call stack.
questions.explanation: Each node adds a frame to the recursion stack.

questions.question: In recursion, why do we need head.next.next = head?
questions.answer: To point the next node back to the current node
questions.explanation: This reverses the direction of the edge between current node and its original successor.

questions.question: After reversing, what does the 'prev' pointer point to?
questions.explanation: Prev finishes at the last non-null node, which becomes the start of the reversed list.

questions.question: Before starting the iterative reversal, 'prev' is initialized to ____.
questions.explanation: The original head will become the new tail, pointing to null.

questions.question: Can you reverse a Doubly Linked List with the same logic?
options: Yes, but you must also swap 'prev' and 'next' pointers for each node
questions.answer: Yes, but you must also swap 'prev' and 'next' pointers for each node
questions.explanation: In DLL, both directions must be updated for every node.

questions.question: To reverse only a portion of the list, we use the ______-pointer technique to find boundaries.
questions.explanation: A dummy node simplifies edge cases like reversing from the first node.

questions.question: What is the base case for recursive reversal?
questions.explanation: Stops when list is empty or reaches the last node.

questions.question: Reversing a list is often a sub-step for checking if a list is a ______.
questions.explanation: Reverse second half and compare with first half.

questions.question: What happens if you forget 'head.next = null' in the recursive version?
questions.answer: A cycle is created between the first two nodes.
questions.explanation: The original head still points to the second node, creating an infinite loop.

questions.question: Which of the following is true for iterative reversal?
options: Modifies the original data in place
questions.answer: Modifies the original data in place
questions.explanation: It changes pointer directions directly in the nodes.

questions.question: The iterative method is generally preferred over recursive because it uses O(__) auxiliary space.
questions.explanation: Recursive uses O(n) stack space.

questions.question: To reverse every 'k' nodes, which data structure is often used as an alternative to pointers?
questions.explanation: Pushing k nodes into a stack and popping them reverses their order easily.

questions.question: In a singly linked list, we can only traverse in ______ direction.
questions.explanation: Unlike doubly linked lists, there are no 'previous' links.

questions.question: Will reversing an empty list crash a well-written code?
questions.explanation: Initial check head == null should handle it.

questions.question: Linked list nodes are stored in ______ memory.
questions.explanation: Nodes are scattered; pointers provide the connection.

questions.question: Tail recursion optimization can make recursive reversal O(__) space in some languages.
questions.explanation: Some compilers reuse stack frames for tail calls.

questions.question: Which data structure is essential for implementing Breadth-First Search?
questions.explanation: BFS explores nodes level by level, requiring a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) structure like a Queue.

questions.question: BFS is primarily used to find the ______ path in an unweighted graph.
questions.explanation: Because it explores all neighbors at distance 1, then distance 2, the first time it reaches a node, it is via the shortest path.

questions.question: Identify the bug: while(q.length > 0) { let u = q.shift(); for(let v of adj[u]) { q.push(v); visited[v] = true; } }
questions.answer: Infinite loop or redundant processing: nodes are added to queue without checking if they were already visited.
questions.explanation: You must check 'if(!visited[v])' before pushing to the queue to avoid cycles and infinite loops.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of BFS using an Adjacency List?
questions.explanation: Every vertex and every edge is explored exactly once in an adjacency list representation.

questions.question: In a BFS traversal, nodes are colored ______ when they are in the queue but not yet processed.
questions.explanation: Standard graph theory coloring: White (unvisited), Gray (discovered/in-queue), Black (processed).

questions.question: BFS can be used to detect which of the following in an undirected graph?
questions.explanation: If BFS encounters an adjacent node that is already 'visited' and is not the parent, a cycle exists.

questions.question: The time complexity of BFS using an Adjacency Matrix is O(____).
questions.explanation: For every node extracted from the queue, we must scan an entire row of size V to find neighbors.

questions.question: Logic check: If I use a Stack instead of a Queue in the BFS code, what does it become?
questions.explanation: Changing the FIFO structure to LIFO changes the traversal logic from level-order to depth-order.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an application of BFS?
options: Solving Rubik's Cube with min moves
questions.explanation: Topological sort is primarily implemented using DFS (Kahn's algorithm uses indegrees, which is BFS-like, but DFS is the standard).

questions.question: BFS on a tree is equivalent to ______ order traversal.
questions.explanation: Both visit nodes level by level starting from the root.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of BFS?
questions.explanation: In the worst case (star graph), the queue can hold almost all vertices at once.

questions.question: A ______ graph is a graph where BFS can find the shortest path without extra weights.
questions.explanation: If weights are present and unequal, Dijkstra's is required.

questions.question: What happens if you don't mark a node as visited until AFTER you shift it from the queue?
questions.explanation: The same node can be added multiple times if reached by different neighbors before being processed.

questions.question: How many times does BFS visit an edge in a directed graph?
questions.explanation: Each directed edge (u, v) is checked exactly once when vertex u is dequeued.

questions.question: BFS starts from a ______ node.
questions.explanation: A starting vertex must be provided to begin the exploration.

questions.question: In 0-1 BFS (edges with weights 0 or 1), what structure is used instead of a standard Queue?
questions.explanation: 0-weight edges are pushed to the front, 1-weight to the back to maintain order in O(V+E).

questions.question: The number of connected components in an undirected graph can be found by calling BFS ______ times.
questions.explanation: Call BFS for every unvisited node until all are marked visited.

questions.question: Can BFS handle cyclic graphs?
questions.explanation: The visited array prevents infinite loops by ensuring each node enters the queue once.

questions.question: Which of these is used in Peer-to-Peer networks for neighbor discovery?
questions.explanation: Nodes broadcast to immediate neighbors, who broadcast further (Gnutella protocol).

questions.question: The maximum distance between any two nodes in a graph is called the ______.
questions.explanation: Can be found using BFS (two passes for trees).

questions.question: What data structure is used for the non-recursive implementation of DFS?
questions.explanation: DFS follows Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) logic to explore deep into a branch before backtracking.

questions.question: DFS uses the ______ strategy to explore a graph.
questions.explanation: It goes as deep as possible and then returns to the previous node to try other branches.

questions.question: Identify the risk in recursive DFS: function dfs(u) { visited[u]=true; for(v of adj[u]) dfs(v); }
questions.answer: Stack Overflow for deep or skewed graphs.
questions.explanation: Recursion depth is limited; for very large graphs, iterative DFS with an explicit stack is safer.

questions.question: Which of these tasks is DFS better at than BFS?
questions.explanation: DFS tracks 'nodes in recursion stack' which makes identifying back-edges (cycles) very easy.

questions.question: The time complexity of DFS using an Adjacency List is O(____).
questions.explanation: Like BFS, it processes every node and every edge once.

questions.question: In DFS, an edge that connects a vertex to its ancestor in the DFS tree is called a:
questions.explanation: A back edge indicates a cycle in the graph.

questions.question: DFS is naturally implemented using ______.
questions.explanation: The system call stack manages the LIFO behavior automatically.

questions.question: Logic check: If a graph has multiple connected components, will one DFS call visit all nodes?
questions.explanation: DFS only visits nodes reachable from the source. A loop is needed to call DFS on all unvisited nodes.

questions.question: Which algorithm uses DFS to find Strongly Connected Components?
questions.explanation: Tarjan's and Kosaraju's both use DFS properties to find SCCs.

questions.question: DFS can produce different results based on the ______ of vertices in the adjacency list.
questions.explanation: The traversal path depends on which neighbor is chosen first.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of DFS?
questions.explanation: We need to store the visited array and the recursion stack (or explicit stack).

questions.question: DFS is used to perform ______ sort on a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).
questions.explanation: Nodes are added to the sort after all their children are visited.

questions.question: Bug check: Marking a node as visited AFTER the recursive call.
questions.explanation: The node must be marked visited BEFORE visiting neighbors to prevent re-visiting the same node.

questions.question: Which of these is used for maze generation?
questions.explanation: Randomized DFS is a very popular maze generation algorithm.

questions.question: The time complexity of DFS with Adjacency Matrix is O(____).
questions.explanation: Requires scanning the entire row for each vertex.

questions.question: In the discovery/finish time property of DFS, if node u is an ancestor of v, then finish[v] is ______ than finish[u].
questions.explanation: The child v must finish its traversal before the parent u can finish.

questions.question: Searching for a specific goal in a very deep or infinite tree may cause DFS to ______.
questions.explanation: It may get stuck in a deep branch even if the goal is near the root in another branch.

questions.question: Does DFS always find the shortest path?
questions.explanation: It finds any path; once it hits the target, it stops, regardless of distance.

questions.question: Which data structure handles backtracking effectively?
questions.explanation: Backtracking is inherently a LIFO process.

questions.question: DFS tree contains forward and cross edges only in ______ graphs.
questions.explanation: Undirected graphs only contain tree and back edges.

questions.question: Which data structure is most efficient for checking balanced parentheses?
questions.explanation: A stack allows tracking the last opened bracket and ensuring it is closed by the correct type.

questions.question: For every closing bracket, we must pop from the stack and check if it ______ the opening bracket.
questions.explanation: For example, ')' must match '('.

questions.question: Identify the bug: if(char == ')') stack.pop(); At the end, if(stack.length == 0) return true;
questions.answer: Fails if stack is empty when ')' appears (underflow).
questions.explanation: You must check if the stack has elements before popping, otherwise a string like '())' might crash or give wrong results.

questions.question: What is the time complexity for checking a string of length n?
questions.explanation: We traverse the string once, performing O(1) stack operations for each character.

questions.question: If the stack is ______ at the end of the string traversal, the parentheses are balanced.
questions.explanation: All opened brackets must have been closed.

questions.question: Which of these strings is balanced?
questions.explanation: Matches correctly in order.

questions.question: Space complexity of this algorithm is O(____).
questions.explanation: Worst case, all characters are opening brackets, filling the stack.

questions.question: Is a hash map useful in this algorithm?
questions.answer: Yes, to store bracket pairs for cleaner matching logic.
questions.explanation: Using a map like {')': '(', ']': '['} simplifies the comparison code.

questions.question: What is the maximum height of the stack for '((()))'?
questions.explanation: Three opening brackets are pushed before the first closing one appears.

questions.question: The balanced parentheses problem is a specific case of the ______ language in formal language theory.
questions.explanation: The Dyck language consists of balanced strings of parentheses.

questions.question: What happens if we encounter '}' but the stack top is '('?
questions.explanation: Brackets must be closed in the correct order of their types.

questions.question: To solve this without a stack for ONLY one type of bracket '()', we can use a simple ______.
questions.explanation: Increment for '(' and decrement for ')'. If counter goes negative or ends non-zero, it's unbalanced.

questions.question: Bug hunt: String '([' is checked. Logic returns true because stack was popped correctly.
questions.answer: Logic error: never checked if stack was empty at the end.
questions.explanation: If characters remain in the stack, it means some brackets were never closed.

questions.question: Which phase of a compiler uses this algorithm?
questions.explanation: Parsing ensuring that code structures (like functions/loops) are properly enclosed.

questions.question: Opening brackets are ______ onto the stack.
questions.explanation: Standard stack operation to store items.

questions.question: Given '((...))' with 100 pairs, how many push operations occur?
questions.explanation: Each opening bracket is pushed exactly once.

questions.question: The time complexity is linear, denoted as O(__).
questions.explanation: n is the number of characters in the string.

questions.question: Can this be solved with a Queue?
questions.explanation: A queue is FIFO; we need to match the MOST RECENT bracket (LIFO).

questions.question: Which bracket is usually checked first?
questions.explanation: We need something in the stack to compare against closing brackets.

questions.question: An algorithm that identifies the minimum number of parentheses to add to make a string balanced also uses a ______.
questions.explanation: The final size of the stack + count of premature closing brackets gives the answer.

questions.question: Radix Sort sorts elements based on which property?
questions.explanation: Radix sort processes numbers digit by digit, from least significant to most significant (or vice versa).

questions.question: The sorting algorithm used as a sub-routine within Radix Sort must be ______.
questions.explanation: Stability is required so that the relative order of elements from previous digit passes is not lost.

questions.question: Find the error: if we sort from Most Significant Digit (MSD) to Least Significant Digit (LSD) without using separate buckets for sub-problems.
questions.answer: The final array will not be sorted correctly.
questions.explanation: LSD works in one pass because it is stable. MSD requires recursive sub-buckets to keep the higher digits in order while sorting lower digits.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Radix Sort for n elements with d digits in base k?
questions.explanation: It takes (n+k) time for each of the d digits using Counting Sort.

questions.question: Radix Sort is a ____-comparative sorting algorithm.
questions.explanation: It does not compare elements against each other; it uses bucket distribution.

questions.question: If n is large and d (number of digits) is small, which algorithm is likely more efficient?
questions.explanation: When d is small, Radix Sort's linear dependency on n outperforms comparison sorts' n log n.

questions.question: LSD in Radix Sort stands for _____ Significant Digit.
questions.explanation: LSD approach starts sorting from the rightmost digit.

questions.question: Can Radix Sort handle variable length strings easily?
questions.answer: Yes, by padding with a null character or using MSD.
questions.explanation: Strings are naturally multi-digit (characters) and can be sorted using Radix logic.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of Radix Sort?
questions.explanation: It requires extra space for the output array and the count (bucket) array.

questions.question: Radix sort can be viewed as a generalization of ______ Sort.
questions.explanation: It distributes elements into buckets multiple times based on digits.

questions.question: What is the base 'k' for decimal numbers in Radix Sort?
questions.explanation: Decimal numbers use digits 0-9, so the bucket range k is 10.

questions.question: In Radix Sort, if integers are sorted in binary, 'k' is equal to ____.
questions.explanation: Binary digits are only 0 and 1.

questions.question: Why is Radix Sort rarely used for sorting floating point numbers?
options: Binary representation of floats is complex to sort bitwise
questions.answer: Binary representation of floats is complex to sort bitwise
questions.explanation: While possible, handling exponents and signs in bitwise Radix Sort requires specialized logic.

questions.question: Which of these is a drawback of Radix Sort?
options: It depends on the range of digits
questions.answer: It depends on the range of digits
questions.explanation: If d is large (e.g. unique long strings), it can be slower than n log n.

questions.question: Counting Sort is the most common ______ used inside Radix Sort.
questions.explanation: Counting sort is linear and stable, making it the perfect helper.

questions.question: How many passes of Counting Sort are needed for numbers up to 999 in base 10?
questions.explanation: One pass for units, one for tens, and one for hundreds.

questions.question: Radix sort is ______-in-place because it needs an output array.
questions.explanation: It is an external/out-of-place algorithm by default.

questions.question: Can Radix Sort handle negative numbers?
questions.answer: Yes, by sorting negatives separately or using an offset.
questions.explanation: Like Counting Sort, standard implementation assumes non-negative indices.

questions.question: Who is credited with the development of Radix Sort?
questions.explanation: Hollerith developed it for use with tabulating machines for the census.

questions.question: The word 'Radix' is another term for the ______ of a number system.
questions.explanation: Base 10 has radix 10.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of the Sliding Window technique?
options: Reducing nested loop O(n^2) to O(n)
questions.answer: Reducing nested loop O(n^2) to O(n)
questions.explanation: It converts a brute force check of all subarrays into a single pass by 'sliding' the range.

questions.question: The two types of sliding windows are Fixed Size and ______ Size.
questions.explanation: Variable windows expand or shrink based on a condition (like sum < k).

questions.question: Find the bug in Fixed Window (sum of k elements): for(i=0; i<n; i++) { sum += arr[i]; if(i >= k) sum -= arr[i-k]; }
questions.answer: No logic error, but it should track max_sum separately.
questions.explanation: This code correctly maintains a sliding sum; you just need to store the maximum seen.

questions.question: Which data structure is typically used for the 'Sliding Window Maximum' problem?
questions.explanation: A Double-Ended Queue (Deque) allows adding/removing from both ends in O(1), maintaining decreasing order of elements.

questions.question: In a variable window, the 'left' pointer moves when the current window ______ the condition.
questions.explanation: If the sum exceeds k, we shrink from the left to regain validity.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the 'Smallest subarray with sum >= S' problem using Sliding Window?
questions.explanation: Although there are two pointers, each pointer visits each element at most once.

questions.question: The sliding window technique is frequently used for ______ and strings.
questions.explanation: Any linear data structure supports contiguous window logic.

questions.question: Is Sliding Window applicable if the problem asks for non-contiguous subsets?
questions.explanation: Sliding window only works for contiguous sub-segments.

questions.question: For 'Longest substring without repeating characters', what extra structure is needed with the window?
questions.explanation: A Set tracks characters currently in the window to detect duplicates.

questions.question: A sliding window problem where we compute the average of every k elements is an example of a ______ average filter.
questions.explanation: Used in signal processing and finance to smooth data.

questions.question: In a fixed window of size 3 on [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], how many windows are there?
To solve sliding window problems with negative numbers, ______ sum with a hash map is often required instead.
questions.explanation: Negative numbers break the monotonic property of simple sliding windows.

questions.question: Bug hunt: while(window_sum > target) { window_sum -= arr[left++]; } Is it safe to return the result inside this loop?
questions.answer: No, result should be updated after the window becomes valid.
questions.explanation: Updating result while the window is still invalid leads to wrong answers.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a sliding window problem?
options: Find max sum subarray of size k
Check if array contains a duplicate
questions.explanation: Merging uses two pointers on different arrays, not a sliding range on one.

questions.question: The time taken to slide the window by one element is O(__).
questions.explanation: We just add the new element and remove the old one.

questions.question: Space complexity for Sliding Window Maximum of window size k?
questions.explanation: The Deque stores at most k indices.

questions.question: Sliding window is an optimization of the ______ force approach.
questions.explanation: It avoids redundant re-calculation of sub-ranges.

questions.question: Does sliding window work on Graphs?
questions.answer: No, generally only on linear sequences.
questions.explanation: Graph windows are non-linear; BFS is used for distance-based levels instead.

questions.question: If window size k = n, the sliding window is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: The window covers the entire dataset and doesn't move.

questions.question: Sliding window technique is a special case of the ______ pointer technique.
questions.explanation: It uses start and end pointers to maintain a range.

questions.question: What is the primary use of a Prefix Sum array?
questions.explanation: Once precomputed, any sum between index i and j can be found in O(1).

questions.question: The formula to find the sum of range [L, R] using prefix sum array P is P[R] - ______.
questions.explanation: We subtract the sum of elements before the starting index L.

questions.question: Identify the bug for range [0, R]: return P[R] - P[-1];
questions.explanation: For L=0, the sum is just P[R]. Code needs a condition or 1-indexed prefix array.

questions.question: What is the time complexity to precompute a Prefix Sum array of size n?
questions.explanation: Each element is visited once and added to the previous sum.

questions.question: Prefix Sum is a form of ______ programming.
questions.explanation: It stores results of sub-problems (sum up to i) to answer global queries.

questions.question: In a 2D matrix, how many Prefix Sum lookups are needed to find a sub-rectangle sum?
Prefix Sum array requires O(__) extra space.
questions.explanation: We must store an additional array of the same size as the input.

questions.question: Can we compute Prefix Sum in-place without an extra array?
questions.explanation: By modifying the original array: arr[i] = arr[i] + arr[i-1].

questions.question: How is the XOR of a range [L, R] calculated using a Prefix XOR array 'PX'?
questions.explanation: Since XOR is its own inverse (A ^ B ^ A = B), the prefix XOR logic follows the same property as prefix sums: to remove the effect of elements before index L, you XOR the prefix sum at R with the prefix sum at L-1.

questions.question: Identify the potential bug when calculating Prefix Sum for an array of 1,000,000 integers, where each integer can be up to 1,000,000: 'int sum = 0; for(int x : arr) { sum += x; prefix.push(sum); }'
questions.explanation: The maximum possible sum (10^6 * 10^6 = 10^12) exceeds the capacity of a standard 32-bit signed integer (approx 2 * 10^9). A 64-bit integer (long/long long) should be used to store the sum.

questions.question: Prefix Sum is most efficient when the number of queries 'Q' is:
questions.explanation: The O(n) precomputation pays off when many O(1) queries follow.

questions.question: Difference Array is a technique often used alongside Prefix Sum to perform range ______ in O(1).
questions.explanation: Update L and R+1 indices, then take prefix sum to apply change to entire range.

questions.question: What is the prefix product array of [1, 2, 3, 4]?
questions.explanation: Prefix product is calculated by multiplying instead of adding.

questions.question: Can Prefix Sum be used to find the average of a range?
options: Only if range size is even
questions.explanation: Calculate range sum in O(1) and divide by the number of elements.

questions.question: The first element of a prefix sum array (P[0]) is always equal to ______.
questions.explanation: Sum up to the first element is the element itself.

questions.question: Which problem can be solved efficiently using Prefix Sum and Hash Maps?
options: Both Subarray with sum 0 and Smallest subarray with sum K
questions.answer: Both Subarray with sum 0 and Smallest subarray with sum K
questions.explanation: If PrefixSum[i] - PrefixSum[j] = K, then the subarray between i and j has sum K.

questions.question: Suffix Sum is the same as Prefix Sum but calculated from ______ to start.
questions.explanation: Accumulating totals from the end of the array.

questions.question: Is Prefix Sum useful if the array is frequently updated?
questions.explanation: Updates take O(n) as all subsequent prefix sums must change. Use Segment Trees or Fenwick Trees instead.

questions.question: Prefix sum is a ______ array.
questions.explanation: Adding non-negative values makes the sum always non-decreasing.

questions.question: The 2D prefix sum technique is also known as the Summed Area ______.
questions.explanation: Frequently used in computer vision (Viola-Jones algorithm).

questions.question: Which algorithm is most famous for detecting a cycle in a linked list?
questions.explanation: It uses two pointers moving at different speeds to find a meeting point.

questions.question: In Floyd's algorithm, the 'Hare' pointer moves ______ steps for every 1 step of the 'Tortoise'.
questions.explanation: The relative speed difference ensures they eventually meet if a cycle exists.

questions.question: Find the bug: while(fast != null) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; if(slow == fast) return true; }
questions.explanation: You must also check if fast.next is null before moving the fast pointer.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of Floyd's Cycle Detection?
questions.explanation: It only requires two pointer variables, regardless of the list size.

questions.question: If the two pointers meet, it is ______ that a cycle exists.
questions.explanation: In a linear list, the fast pointer would simply hit null.

questions.question: To find the START of the cycle after the pointers meet, where should you reset one pointer?
questions.explanation: Move one to head and keep other at meeting point. Move both at speed 1; they will meet at the start of the cycle.

questions.question: An alternative to Floyd's is to use a ______ to store visited nodes.
questions.explanation: If you encounter a node already in the set, a cycle is present.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the Hash Set approach?
questions.explanation: We visit each node once and check the set in O(1).

questions.question: What is the space complexity of the Hash Set approach?
questions.explanation: In the worst case, we store all n nodes in the set.

questions.question: The mathematical proof for finding the cycle start is based on the equation L = ______, where L is distance to cycle and nC is cycle length.
questions.explanation: Refers to the distance from meeting point to cycle start.

questions.question: Will Floyd's algorithm work if the Hare moves 3 steps instead of 2?
questions.explanation: Any difference in speed will eventually lead to a meeting if the path is closed.

questions.question: A linked list where the last node points to the head is called a ______ linked list.
questions.explanation: This is a special case of a cycle.

questions.question: Bug hunt: slow = head; fast = head.next; while(slow != fast) { ... } What if head is null?
questions.explanation: Initial check head == null || head.next == null is required.

questions.question: Time complexity of Floyd's Cycle Detection?
questions.explanation: The hare will complete at most two laps before meeting the tortoise.

questions.question: The fast pointer is the hare, and the ______ pointer is the tortoise.
questions.explanation: Standard naming for the two pointers.

questions.question: Brent's algorithm for cycle detection is generally ______ than Floyd's.
questions.explanation: Brent's uses power-of-two increments and performs fewer total steps.

questions.question: After finding a cycle, the length of the cycle can be found by keeping one pointer fixed and moving the other until they ______.
questions.explanation: Count steps in one lap of the cycle.

questions.question: Can cycle detection be used on a Doubly Linked List?
questions.explanation: The logic is independent of back-pointers.

questions.question: If there is no cycle, the fast pointer will eventually reach:
questions.explanation: End of a standard linear list.

questions.question: To remove the cycle, find the node ______ the cycle start and set its next to null.
questions.explanation: The last node in the cycle must be unlinked.

questions.question: What is the primary goal of the Two-Pointer technique?
options: To sort an array in O(n log n)
To reduce O(n²) complexity to O(n)
To search for elements in a BST
To reverse a string in O(log n)
questions.answer: To reduce O(n²) complexity to O(n)
questions.explanation: By using two pointers moving toward each other or at different speeds, we avoid nested iterations.

questions.question: For a sorted array, to find a pair with sum K, we place pointers at the ______ and ______.
questions.explanation: We adjust pointers inward based on whether the current sum is smaller or larger than K.

questions.question: Bug hunt: while(left < right) { sum = a[left] + a[right]; if(sum == K) return true; if(sum < K) right--; else left++; }
questions.explanation: If sum < K, we need a larger sum, so move left++. If sum > K, move right--.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a variation of the Two-Pointer technique?
questions.explanation: Level-order uses a queue, not pointers within a linear sequence.

questions.question: The ______ speed pointer variation is used to find the middle of a linked list.
questions.explanation: A fast pointer moves twice as fast as the slow pointer.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the '3Sum' problem using Two-Pointer on a sorted array?
questions.explanation: One outer loop and one nested two-pointer search results in quadratic time.

questions.question: The two-pointer technique is primarily applied to ______ and linked lists.
